quiz: Interviewers will dig into the project for half an hour. Ask which quality lets you answer every why from memory.
Each letter is one part of the walkthrough, in the order you would tell it. Think story of a project, not a release process.
An overview should be readable at a glance, like a subway map. Too few hides the flow, too many hides the decision.
A strong result names a metric, the before and after values, and where the numbers came from.
Neither ego nor surrender helps. Pick the reaction that shows you weighed the option and had reasons.
Interviewers keep digging until you reach an edge. Think about which behaviour there keeps their trust.
It is a four-step pattern for a mistake story: what happened, how bad, what you did right away, what changed for good.
The panel is scoring one person, not the team. Think about which sentences tell them what you did.
Most of the depth signal comes out when panelists ask questions. How much room should you leave for that?
Staff scope is less about code volume and more about direction across several teams.
Think about how you would separate your change from everything else that happened in the same weeks.
Avoid both extremes: no reflection at all, or trashing your own work. Look for specific, tied-to-pain changes.
Panels accept abstraction but judge discretion. Which option protects secrets while still telling the story?
interview: Use the seven-part skeleton with a roadmap sentence first, and put a number in both the problem and the result.
Name the real alternatives, what mattered most, why one option won, and the cost you knowingly accepted.
Give team size and the split early, then switch to I for your own decisions and credit others by name.
Cover the metric definition, data source, comparison window, and how you ruled out other causes.
Pick a real mistake you personally made and walk through impact in numbers, the quick fix, and lasting prevention.
Avoid saying nothing or everything. Pick one or two changes linked to real pain and the habit you have now.
Stateless parts scale easily. Do the arithmetic on the stateful or rate-limited parts to find the first to saturate.
Admit the boundary, reason from what you do know, and say exactly how you would confirm it.
Think of a scorecard: ownership, depth, measurable result, recency, level fit and some tension. Prepare a backup too.
Lead with the organisational problem and how you shaped it; show leverage through others while keeping technical depth.
Agree with the general principle first, then give your specific constraint, admit the cost, and say when you would choose differently.
Draw a few boxes left to right while talking, label arrows with sync or async and scale, and mark your own parts.
State the outcome early, show what was strong, find the root cause, and own your part in it with a lasting lesson.
Be precise about what you designed versus what was generated, and show that you can defend and own every line.
